content: Acetyl, also known as ethanoyl in organic chemistry, is a functional group derived from acetic acid. Its chemical formula is -COCH3. It is often abbreviated as Ac, though this should not be confused with the element actinium. The acetyl radical consists of a methyl group that is single-bonded to a carbonyl group. The carbon atom in the carbonyl group has a lone electron available, which allows it to form a chemical bond with the remainder of the molecule, denoted as R. Acetyl groups are integral components of numerous organic compounds, including the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, acetyl-CoA, and the analgesics acetaminophen and acetylsalicylic acid (commonly known as aspirin). The process of introducing an acetyl group into a molecule is referred to as acetylation, or ethanoylation. In biological systems, acetyl groups are frequently transferred while bound to Coenzyme A (CoA) in the form of acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA serves as a critical intermediate in both the synthesis and breakdown of various organic molecules. Additionally, acetyl groups are often added to histones and other proteins, altering their properties. For instance, at the DNA level, histone acetylation by acetyltransferases (HATs) leads to an expansion of chromatin structure, which facilitates genetic transcription. Conversely, the removal of acetyl groups by histone deacetylases (HDACs) results in the condensation of DNA structure, thereby inhibiting transcription. When acetyl groups are attached to certain organic molecules, they enhance the molecule's ability to cross the blood-brain barrier. This property allows drugs to reach the brain more rapidly, intensifying their effects and increasing the efficacy of a given dose. For example, acetyl groups are used to convert the natural anti-inflammatory compound salicylic acid into the more effective acetylsalicylic acid, or aspirin. Similarly, acetylation transforms the natural painkiller morphine into diacetylmorphine, commonly known as heroin.
